blocks.text: **The problem.** Given an array `nums` of size `n`, return the **majority element** — the value that appears **more than n / 2 times**. You may assume a majority element always exists.

blocks.alt: The array [2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2]. The four 2s are highlighted: 2 appears 4 times out of 7, which is more than half.

elements.text: 2 appears 4 times, n / 2 = 3.5  →  2 is the majority
elements.originalText: 2 appears 4 times, n / 2 = 3.5  →  2 is the majority

blocks.code:
Input:  nums = [3, 2, 3]
Output: 3

Input:  nums = [2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2]
Output: 2

blocks.text: "More than half" is a strong promise: the majority value outnumbers **all the other values put together**. Keep that sentence in mind — the best solution is built entirely on it.
For each element, count how many times it appears by scanning the whole array. The first one whose count passes `n / 2` is the answer.
**Time O(n²), space O(1).** The same values get counted over and over.
2. Optimal: count once with a hash map
Keep a running count per value in a hash map. As soon as a count passes `n / 2`, that value is the majority.

**Time O(n), space O(n).** One pass — but the map can hold up to n/2 different values. (Sorting and taking the middle element also works, since the majority must cover the middle, but that costs O(n log n).)
3. Best solution: let the votes cancel out (Boyer–Moore)

Imagine every element is a voter. Pair up two **different** values and remove them both — one majority vote and one other vote cancel. Because the majority has more votes than everyone else combined, it can never be cancelled completely: whatever survives at the end must be the majority.

blocks.alt: Pairing different values: each 1 is paired with a 2 and both are crossed out. One 2 is left over, so 2 is the majority.

elements.text: … and a 2 is still left over
elements.originalText: … and a 2 is still left over

blocks.text: The cancelling takes one pass and two variables, a `candidate` and its `count`:

items: If `count` is 0, nobody is ahead — the current value becomes the new `candidate`.
If the current value equals the candidate, `count` goes up by one (a supporting vote).
Otherwise `count` goes down by one (a vote cancelled).

blocks.alt: A trace table of Boyer–Moore voting on [2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2] with columns i, value, candidate, count. The candidate ends as 2.
blocks.caption: 1 briefly takes the lead, and 2 still wins at the end.
Try [1, 3, 3, 2, 3, 3, 3], where the majority only takes over late. With no majority at all, you'll see why the problem's guarantee matters.

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(1).** One pass, two variables.

blocks.alt: Brute force: O(n²) time, O(1) space. Optimal: O(n) time, O(n) space. Best: O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: **If a majority isn't guaranteed**, count the final candidate in a second pass and only return it if it really appears more than n / 2 times.

blocks.text: The follow-up "find every value that appears more than **n / 3** times" uses the same cancelling idea with **two** candidates and two counts — at most two values can pass n / 3.
